unit-m32.title: Topic 3 · 3-2 Place Value Through Millions
unit-m32.source: enVision Math, Topic 3 textbook scan — Lessons 3-1 to 3-7 (Drive)

summary.text: Lesson 3-2 extends the place-value chart through the millions: reading and writing numbers in standard form, expanded form and number names, and the rule that a digit one place left is worth 10 times as much — with the factors stacking when places are further apart.

why.text: Every skill in this topic — decimals, comparing, rounding — is the same chart read further right. Getting the ×10-per-seat rule solid on whole numbers now makes the decimal version feel like the same fact instead of a new one.

objectives.text: Read and write numbers through the millions in standard form, expanded form and words.
State the value of any digit from its place.
Compare two identical digits in different places and give the exact factor between them.

parentNote.text: The trap in this lesson is the ×10 rule applied without counting seats — two 6s that sit two places apart differ by 100 times, not 10. One question makes her verify a CORRECT expanded form, because confirming right answers is rarer practice than catching wrong ones.

nextUp.text: Cards, then the quiz. If the 10-times questions feel slippery, the fifth card is the one to re-read.

cards.def:
**The value of a digit depends on WHERE it sits in the number.**
• In 5,283 the 5 is worth 5,000 — not 5.
• The chart runs ones, tens, hundreds, thousands… up through millions.
cards.hint: Same digit, different seat, different value.

cards.def:
**Groups of three places separated by commas: ones, thousands, millions.**
• 22,000,000 reads by periods: twenty-two million.
• Commas are there to let your eyes find the periods fast.
cards.hint: Read big numbers in threes, comma to comma.

cards.def:
**The number written as a sum of each digit times its place value.**
• 3,514 = 3,000 + 500 + 10 + 4.
• With exponents: (3 × 10³) + (5 × 10²) + (1 × 10¹) + (4 × 1).
cards.hint: Pull the number apart seat by seat.

cards.def:
**The number written in words, period by period.**
• 4,070,000 is "four million, seventy thousand".
• A zero in a place means that place is silent — you never say it.
cards.hint: Say each period, then its name: million, thousand.

cards.def:
**A digit one place to the LEFT is worth 10 times as much.**
• In 7,700 the left 7 (thousands) is worth 10 times the right 7 (hundreds).
• Two places apart means 10 × 10 = 100 times — the places multiply.
cards.hint: Every step left is one ×10. Steps stack.

questions.q: A stadium sold 3,000,000 tickets over its lifetime. What is the number name for 3,000,000?
questions.hint: Count off the periods from the right: ones, thousands, millions.
steps: Group by commas: 3 | 000 | 000.
The 3 sits in the millions period.
So the name is three million.

ex.main: **Three million.** Two full periods of zeros after the 3 puts it in the millions.
ex.tip: Commas are not decoration — they name the periods for you.

questions.q: What is the value of the 8 in 4,829,157?
questions.hint: Find the 8's seat first, then its value.
steps: Count places from the right: 7 ones, 5 tens, 1 hundreds, 9 thousands, 2 ten-thousands, 8 hundred-thousands.
The 8 sits in the hundred-thousands place.

ex.main: **800,000.** The digit is 8, but the seat makes it eight hundred thousand.
ex.tip: Digit and value are different questions — the seat does the multiplying.

questions.q: Which number has a 6 in the ten-thousands place?
questions.hint: Ten-thousands is the fifth seat from the right.
steps: Count five places from the right in each number.
In 165,204 the fifth digit from the right is 6.
The others put the 6 in a different seat or not at all in that one.

ex.main: **165,204.** Fifth place from the right — count seats, do not eyeball.
ex.tip: Counting from the right never lies; guessing from the left often does.

questions.q: Which is the standard form of (7 × 10⁶) + (2 × 10⁴) + (5 × 10²)?
questions.hint: Give every silent place its zero.
steps: Add them, keeping zeros in the empty seats: 7,020,500.

ex.main: **7,020,500.** The places with no term still need their zeros.
ex.tip: Expanded form only lists the seats that are filled — standard form shows every seat.

questions.q: An ant colony can hold about twenty-two million ants. How is that written in standard form?
questions.hint: Millions is a whole period — three zeros twice.
steps: Twenty-two goes in the millions period: 22.
The thousands and ones periods are empty: 000 and 000.

ex.main: **22,000,000.** Two full periods of zeros carry the 22 up to millions.
ex.tip: Standard form is just the name translated seat by seat.

questions.q: In the number 5,500, how does the value of the left 5 compare to the right 5?
questions.hint: How many seats apart are the two 5s?
steps: The left 5 is in the thousands place: 5,000.
The right 5 is in the hundreds place: 500.
5,000 ÷ 500 = 10 — one seat apart, one ×10.

ex.main: **10 times as great.** Adjacent places always differ by a factor of 10.
ex.tip: This ×10-per-seat rule is the whole reason the decimal system works.

questions.q: Mara says that in 6,367, one 6 is 10 times as great as the other. What should you tell her?
opts: The two 6s are equal because they are the same digit
She is right — neighbouring 6s always differ by 10 times
The 6s are two places apart, so the left one is 100 times as great
The left 6 is 1,000 times as great
steps: The left 6 is in the thousands place: 6,000.
The right 6 is in the tens place: 60.
They are two seats apart, so the factor is 10 × 10 = 100.

ex.main: **100 times, not 10.** The ×10 rule is per seat, and these 6s are two seats apart.
ex.tip: The rule she remembered is right — she skipped counting the seats between.

questions.q: A 4-digit number has all four digits the same, and the digit in the hundreds place is worth 200. What is the number?
questions.hint: What digit makes the hundreds place worth 200?
steps: Hundreds worth 200 means the digit is 2.
All four digits are the same, so every digit is 2.
The number is 2,222.

ex.main: **2,222.** One clue about one seat, plus "all the same", pins every digit.
ex.tip: Each 2 in 2,222 is worth 10 times its right-hand neighbour: 2,000, 200, 20, 2.

questions.q: Ben writes the expanded form of two million, forty thousand, six as (2 × 10⁶) + (4 × 10⁴) + 6. Did he get it right?
opts: Yes — each part lands in the correct place
questions.hint: Check each part against its place value.
steps: Forty thousand = 40,000 = 4 × 10⁴. ✓
Six ones = 6. ✓
Standard form: 2,040,006.

ex.main: **Yes.** Every term matches its seat — the number is 2,040,006.
ex.tip: Verifying someone right is the same skill as catching them wrong: check seat by seat.

questions.q: Which number is 100 times as great as 3,070?
questions.hint: Two ×10 steps — every digit moves two seats left.
steps: 100 times = two place-value steps left.

ex.main: **307,000.** Multiplying by 100 slides the whole number two seats left.
ex.tip: The digits never change — only their seats do.
